what_it_does: When engineers design high-frequency circuits (think chips, antennas, or circuit boards that operate at gigahertz speeds), they often need compact mathematical models — called S-parameter macromodels — that accurately describe how electrical signals flow through a component. One physical requirement these models must satisfy is 'passivity': the model must not predict that a passive component generates energy on its own, which would be physically impossible. Enforcing passivity after fitting a model is a hard optimization problem that tends to be slow and memory-hungry. This paper reframes the passivity-enforcement step as training a neural network (a layered mathematical function inspired loosely by the brain), so that it can exploit the massively parallel arithmetic hardware inside a modern graphics card (GPU) to run the optimization much faster and with less memory. The abstract does not quantify the speedup or detail the network architecture.
